newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US, BOJ rumors kill rally vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US, BOJ rumors kill rally vs yen.

text.p: The dollar closed higher versus the mark but talk of Japanese central bank sales squashed an early rally against the yen.

The dollar advanced broadly early Thursday, lifted by remarks from a German central banker, which weakened the mark, and rumors that a newsletter released by a popular Washington-based consulting firm said the U.S. government could tolerate the dollar strengthening to 120 versus the yen.
But traders, already on tenterhooks after Japan's Finance Minister carped about the yen's recent slide again during Tokyo trading, soon discounted the newsletter talk.

The Japanese central bank declined to comment on rumors it had sold dollars near 117.30 yen after the start of the U.S. session. But the intervention talk checked the dollar's early advance short of Wednesday's 45-month high near 117.50 yen.

"I can not confirm anything; I don't know if anybody can," said John McCarthy, of ING Barings Capital Markets in New York. "Obviously there was some selling interest driving it all the way down (to 116.25 yen). It is still very heavy."
The dollar ended at 116.60/65 yen down from 117.05/15 at the open and at 1.5945/55 marks, up from 1.5930/40.

Commenting on the dollar's rise to 117.48 on Wednesday, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, said on Thursday it is not desirable for the foreign exchange rate to fluctuate wildly, and that the excessive yen depreciation is undesirable.

Concerns that Japanese government proposals to implement budget belt-tightening this spring could derail an already fragile economy sent Japan's stock market into a tailspin last week and the yen has tumbled since the beginning of the year.
Foreigners have exacerbated the yen's slide by selling Japanese assets and then exchanging the revenues for other currencies.

"Utlimately we'll probably see Japan intervene in some protracted fashion, because there is very little reason at this stage to own yen," said David Gilmore, partner at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.
The mark slumped against many currencies, including the dollar, after remarks from Hans-Juergen Krupp, who sits on the Bundesbank's policy-making council.
Dollar/mark hit a high of 1.5970 in the U.S. The mark also took it on the chin against the yen and some European currencies, notably Norway's crown, on Thursday.
At a speech in Hamburg, Krupp said the record rate of German joblessness proved the economy was in a grave position and the German central bank could not be indifferent to this.
"That would be probably be one of the reasons why the dollar popped up and I think that is one reason why the mark is under so much pressure," said McCarthy.
The dollar reached a 30-month high at 1.6001 marks on Wednesday, fueled in part by speculation the Bundesbank might trim interest rates to stimulate Germany's weak economy.

"I think the outlook is just so rosy on the U.S. economy and not so on Germany that it just seems to be a natural play people want to make," said John Beerling, chief dealer at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.

In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.3762/72 Swiss francs from 1.3770/80 at the open. It rose to Canadian $1.3410/15 from C$1.3382/87. The pound rose to $1.6790/00 from $1.6772/82 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7792/97 from $0.7777/82.
